<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p01" data-practice-set="P01" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p01-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> A club overlooks renting equipment, exaggerates the durability of buying, and never decides how much storage space matters. Which sequence names these three problems?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-01-a" name="p01-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Valuation, prediction, implementation</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-01-b" name="p01-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Implementation, learning, prediction</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-01-c" name="p01-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Learning, option construction, valuation</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-01-d" name="p01-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Prediction, valuation, option construction</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-01-e" name="p01-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Option construction, prediction, valuation</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> A family tradition makes a meal feel especially valuable to one person. Which conclusion distinguishes explanation from normative evaluation?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-02-a" name="p01-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> An inherited tradition determines the ethically best meal for everyone.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-02-b" name="p01-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> A meal has value only through its market price.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-02-c" name="p01-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A culturally learned value cannot influence a real preference.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-02-d" name="p01-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The tradition helps explain the value; it does not settle what everyone ought to choose.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-02-e" name="p01-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> A utility representation must ignore the meal&#x27;s social meaning.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> A job comparison page makes salary prominent and hides commuting time. Applicants focus on salary. Which redesign best addresses the resulting comparison problem?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-03-a" name="p01-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Explain the selected job only after the contract is signed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-03-b" name="p01-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Ask applicants to ignore their personal travel preferences.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-03-c" name="p01-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Increase the prominence of the highest salary further.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-03-d" name="p01-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Show salary and commuting time together on clearly labeled scales.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-03-e" name="p01-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Remove salary so that commuting becomes the only visible attribute.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> A supplier recommendation reverses if an uncertain failure rate rises from 3% to 4%, both plausible values. The choice is costly to reverse. A quick, inexpensive check could substantially improve the estimate. What analysis is most valuable next?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-04-a" name="p01-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Treat the central estimate as certain because it fits the current model.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-04-b" name="p01-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Refine an unrelated estimate that leaves the recommendation unchanged.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-04-c" name="p01-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Improve the consequential failure-rate estimate and compare outcomes across its plausible range.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-04-d" name="p01-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Average the suppliers&#x27; names to remove personal preference.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-04-e" name="p01-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Stop analysis because a numerical recommendation already exists.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> A coach predicts an athlete will excel and gives that athlete extra practice. Later success is treated as proof that the coach merely recognized innate ability. What has been overlooked?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-05-a" name="p01-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> The prediction may have altered the athlete&#x27;s learning environment.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-05-b" name="p01-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> The prediction must have been consciously insincere.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-05-c" name="p01-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A correct forecast rules out effects of the coach&#x27;s actions.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-05-d" name="p01-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Practice cannot be measured as part of a causal pathway.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-05-e" name="p01-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The outcome supplies a direct measure of innate ability alone.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> Customers give higher ratings to coffee sold at higher prices, but both the coffees and customers differ. Which follow-up best separates a price-induced expectation effect from a physical coffee difference?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-06-a" name="p01-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Compare premium beans with cheaper beans at their usual prices.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-06-b" name="p01-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Replace tasting ratings with the retailer&#x27;s preferred price.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-06-c" name="p01-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Randomly assign price labels to tasters served the same coffee.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-06-d" name="p01-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Change both the price and serving temperature.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-06-e" name="p01-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Ask only participants who already prefer expensive coffee.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> A person recognizes a blurred face using context, then forecasts that the recognized person will accept an invitation. Later she explains why she had expected acceptance. Which distinction best organizes the sequence?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-07-a" name="p01-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> An action, an outcome, then a controlled experiment</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-07-b" name="p01-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Perceptual inference, consequence forecast, then retrospective explanation</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-07-c" name="p01-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A consequence forecast followed by two perceptual inferences</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-07-d" name="p01-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Three direct recordings of external reality</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-07-e" name="p01-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Three judgments of the invitation&#x27;s monetary value</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> A job seeker initially compares salary alone. She then discovers that one employer will trade a little salary for flexible hours, which she values highly. What should she do next?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-08-a" name="p01-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Choose the higher salary because only money is comparable.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-08-b" name="p01-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Assume flexibility has the same value for every applicant.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-08-c" name="p01-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Infer that the employer&#x27;s first offer was irrational.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-08-d" name="p01-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Evaluate the newly feasible salary–hours package against alternatives.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-08-e" name="p01-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Treat the original salary as a cost already paid.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> An expected-profit maximizer can take a certain €50 or launch a product earning €120 on success and €0 otherwise; success has probability 0.4. Perfect information costs €15 and arrives before the choice; both actions remain available. What policy maximizes expected net profit?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-09-a" name="p01-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Buy information; launch only on success, otherwise take €50.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-09-b" name="p01-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Decline information and launch the product.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-09-c" name="p01-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Buy information and launch regardless of its result.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-09-d" name="p01-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Buy information and take €50 regardless of its result.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-09-e" name="p01-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Decline information and take €50.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p01-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p01-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> A randomized label study detects a change in reported enjoyment but no reliable performance difference. Participants later say the label helped concentration; concentration was not independently measured. Which claim best fits?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p01-10-a" name="p01-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> The label had no effect on any unmeasured experience.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p01-10-b" name="p01-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> The label changed performance despite the reported comparison.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p01-10-c" name="p01-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> The label changed concentration, which mediated the rating effect.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p01-10-d" name="p01-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The retrospective account identifies the participants&#x27; original causal process.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p01-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p01-10-e" name="p01-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The label changed reported enjoyment; the concentration mechanism remains untested.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p01-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>

<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p01"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p01-01"><h3>Question 1: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Valuation, prediction, implementation <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The first is omission of an option; the third is weighting a consequence.</dd>
<dt>B. Implementation, learning, prediction <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The problems arise before implementation or outcome feedback.</dd>
<dt>C. Learning, option construction, valuation <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The first problem is not learning from an outcome.</dd>
<dt>D. Prediction, valuation, option construction <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This shifts each problem to the wrong stage.</dd>
<dt>E. Option construction, prediction, valuation <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The problems concern alternatives, consequences, and their importance respectively.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/01-understanding-decision-making.html">Chapter 1</a> · <a href="../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.html">Chapter 2</a>. <a href="#p01-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p01-02"><h3>Question 2: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. An inherited tradition determines the ethically best meal for everyone. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Origins do not establish universal moral worth.</dd>
<dt>B. A meal has value only through its market price. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Valuation also reflects identity, relationships, and experience.</dd>
<dt>C. A culturally learned value cannot influence a real preference. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Learned meanings can shape subjective value.</dd>
<dt>D. The tradition helps explain the value; it does not settle what everyone ought to choose. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Socially acquired meaning explains preferences without supplying a universal prescription.</dd>
<dt>E. A utility representation must ignore the meal&#x27;s social meaning. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Preference ordering can reflect consequences with social meaning.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/01-understanding-decision-making.html">Chapter 1</a> · <a href="../chapters/06-valuation.html">Chapter 6</a>. <a href="#p01-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p01-03"><h3>Question 3: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Explain the selected job only after the contract is signed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Later justification does not repair the original comparison.</dd>
<dt>B. Ask applicants to ignore their personal travel preferences. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Preferences over commuting remain relevant.</dd>
<dt>C. Increase the prominence of the highest salary further. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This intensifies the original attentional imbalance.</dd>
<dt>D. Show salary and commuting time together on clearly labeled scales. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Making both consequences interpretable helps them enter valuation.</dd>
<dt>E. Remove salary so that commuting becomes the only visible attribute. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>That replaces one incomplete comparison with another.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/03-limited-attention.html">Chapter 3</a> · <a href="../chapters/06-valuation.html">Chapter 6</a>. <a href="#p01-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p01-04"><h3>Question 4: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Treat the central estimate as certain because it fits the current model. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A plausible model prediction still carries uncertainty.</dd>
<dt>B. Refine an unrelated estimate that leaves the recommendation unchanged. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Precision in an inconsequential input has less decision value.</dd>
<dt>C. Improve the consequential failure-rate estimate and compare outcomes across its plausible range. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The consequential sensitivity and inexpensive informative check make this uncertainty worth investigating.</dd>
<dt>D. Average the suppliers&#x27; names to remove personal preference. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The issue is uncertainty about consequences, not naming.</dd>
<dt>E. Stop analysis because a numerical recommendation already exists. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A fragile consequential recommendation warrants a proportionate check.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.html">Chapter 2</a> · <a href="../chapters/04-predictive-mind.html">Chapter 4</a>. <a href="#p01-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p01-05"><h3>Question 5: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. The prediction may have altered the athlete&#x27;s learning environment. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Treatment induced by a forecast can help cause the outcome.</dd>
<dt>B. The prediction must have been consciously insincere. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The coach can sincerely believe the forecast.</dd>
<dt>C. A correct forecast rules out effects of the coach&#x27;s actions. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Predictive success and causal influence can coexist.</dd>
<dt>D. Practice cannot be measured as part of a causal pathway. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Practice is precisely a potentially measurable mediator.</dd>
<dt>E. The outcome supplies a direct measure of innate ability alone. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Changed opportunities prevent that simple interpretation.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/04-predictive-mind.html">Chapter 4</a> · <a href="../chapters/05-expectations.html">Chapter 5</a>. <a href="#p01-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p01-06"><h3>Question 6: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Compare premium beans with cheaper beans at their usual prices. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Physical quality and price then vary together.</dd>
<dt>B. Replace tasting ratings with the retailer&#x27;s preferred price. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A preferred price does not measure the experience under study.</dd>
<dt>C. Randomly assign price labels to tasters served the same coffee. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Identical coffee and random labels isolate the label manipulation.</dd>
<dt>D. Change both the price and serving temperature. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Temperature becomes an additional explanation.</dd>
<dt>E. Ask only participants who already prefer expensive coffee. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Selection limits the comparison and does not isolate the manipulation.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/04-predictive-mind.html">Chapter 4</a> · <a href="../chapters/06-valuation.html">Chapter 6</a>. <a href="#p01-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p01-07"><h3>Question 7: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. An action, an outcome, then a controlled experiment <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No controlled manipulation is described.</dd>
<dt>B. Perceptual inference, consequence forecast, then retrospective explanation <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The stages answer what is present, what will happen, and why a prior judgment was made.</dd>
<dt>C. A consequence forecast followed by two perceptual inferences <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Recognition comes first, and the final account concerns a prior judgment.</dd>
<dt>D. Three direct recordings of external reality <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Inference, forecasting, and explanation all involve interpretation.</dd>
<dt>E. Three judgments of the invitation&#x27;s monetary value <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>None is necessarily a valuation in money.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/04-predictive-mind.html">Chapter 4</a> · <a href="../chapters/07-rationalization.html">Chapter 7</a>. <a href="#p01-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p01-08"><h3>Question 8: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Choose the higher salary because only money is comparable. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Nonmonetary consequences can be valued and compared.</dd>
<dt>B. Assume flexibility has the same value for every applicant. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The chapter emphasizes differences in subjective value.</dd>
<dt>C. Infer that the employer&#x27;s first offer was irrational. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Negotiability does not establish irrationality.</dd>
<dt>D. Evaluate the newly feasible salary–hours package against alternatives. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Option construction and valuation should incorporate the negotiable trade-off.</dd>
<dt>E. Treat the original salary as a cost already paid. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>An offer is not an incurred sunk cost.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.html">Chapter 2</a> · <a href="../chapters/06-valuation.html">Chapter 6</a>. <a href="#p01-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p01-09"><h3>Question 9: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Buy information; launch only on success, otherwise take €50. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Perfect information yields 0.4×120 + 0.6×50 − 15 = €63, above €50.</dd>
<dt>B. Decline information and launch the product. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Its expected profit is €48, below the certain €50.</dd>
<dt>C. Buy information and launch regardless of its result. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This earns €48 − €15 = €33 in expectation.</dd>
<dt>D. Buy information and take €50 regardless of its result. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This earns €35 and wastes the information.</dd>
<dt>E. Decline information and take €50. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This misses the available €63 expected net payoff.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.html">Chapter 2</a> · <a href="../appendices/appendix-a-rational-choice-and-decision-analysis.html">Appendix A: decision analysis</a>. <a href="#p01-09">Back to question 9</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p01-10"><h3>Question 10: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. The label had no effect on any unmeasured experience. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Lack of measurement cannot establish no effect.</dd>
<dt>B. The label changed performance despite the reported comparison. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The study did not reliably detect that difference.</dd>

<dt>D. The retrospective account identifies the participants&#x27; original causal process. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A sincere account can be a post hoc explanation.</dd>
<dt>E. The label changed reported enjoyment; the concentration mechanism remains untested. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The outcome comparison supports the rating effect, not the retrospective causal account.</dd>

::: {.content-visible when-format="epub"}
Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p01-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** A club overlooks renting equipment, exaggerates the durability of buying, and never decides how much storage space matters. Which sequence names these three problems?

A) Valuation, prediction, implementation
B) Implementation, learning, prediction
C) Learning, option construction, valuation
D) Prediction, valuation, option construction
E) Option construction, prediction, valuation

:::

::: {#p01-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** A family tradition makes a meal feel especially valuable to one person. Which conclusion distinguishes explanation from normative evaluation?

A) An inherited tradition determines the ethically best meal for everyone.
B) A meal has value only through its market price.
C) A culturally learned value cannot influence a real preference.
D) The tradition helps explain the value; it does not settle what everyone ought to choose.
E) A utility representation must ignore the meal's social meaning.

:::

::: {#p01-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** A job comparison page makes salary prominent and hides commuting time. Applicants focus on salary. Which redesign best addresses the resulting comparison problem?

A) Explain the selected job only after the contract is signed.
B) Ask applicants to ignore their personal travel preferences.
C) Increase the prominence of the highest salary further.
D) Show salary and commuting time together on clearly labeled scales.
E) Remove salary so that commuting becomes the only visible attribute.

:::

::: {#p01-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A supplier recommendation reverses if an uncertain failure rate rises from 3% to 4%, both plausible values. The choice is costly to reverse. A quick, inexpensive check could substantially improve the estimate. What analysis is most valuable next?

A) Treat the central estimate as certain because it fits the current model.
B) Refine an unrelated estimate that leaves the recommendation unchanged.
C) Improve the consequential failure-rate estimate and compare outcomes across its plausible range.
D) Average the suppliers' names to remove personal preference.
E) Stop analysis because a numerical recommendation already exists.

:::

::: {#p01-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** A coach predicts an athlete will excel and gives that athlete extra practice. Later success is treated as proof that the coach merely recognized innate ability. What has been overlooked?

A) The prediction may have altered the athlete's learning environment.
B) The prediction must have been consciously insincere.
C) A correct forecast rules out effects of the coach's actions.
D) Practice cannot be measured as part of a causal pathway.
E) The outcome supplies a direct measure of innate ability alone.

:::

::: {#p01-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** Customers give higher ratings to coffee sold at higher prices, but both the coffees and customers differ. Which follow-up best separates a price-induced expectation effect from a physical coffee difference?

A) Compare premium beans with cheaper beans at their usual prices.
B) Replace tasting ratings with the retailer's preferred price.
C) Randomly assign price labels to tasters served the same coffee.
D) Change both the price and serving temperature.
E) Ask only participants who already prefer expensive coffee.

:::

::: {#p01-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** A person recognizes a blurred face using context, then forecasts that the recognized person will accept an invitation. Later she explains why she had expected acceptance. Which distinction best organizes the sequence?

A) An action, an outcome, then a controlled experiment
B) Perceptual inference, consequence forecast, then retrospective explanation
C) A consequence forecast followed by two perceptual inferences
D) Three direct recordings of external reality
E) Three judgments of the invitation's monetary value

:::

::: {#p01-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** A job seeker initially compares salary alone. She then discovers that one employer will trade a little salary for flexible hours, which she values highly. What should she do next?

A) Choose the higher salary because only money is comparable.
B) Assume flexibility has the same value for every applicant.
C) Infer that the employer's first offer was irrational.
D) Evaluate the newly feasible salary–hours package against alternatives.
E) Treat the original salary as a cost already paid.

:::

::: {#p01-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** An expected-profit maximizer can take a certain €50 or launch a product earning €120 on success and €0 otherwise; success has probability 0.4. Perfect information costs €15 and arrives before the choice; both actions remain available. What policy maximizes expected net profit?

A) Buy information; launch only on success, otherwise take €50.
B) Decline information and launch the product.
C) Buy information and launch regardless of its result.
D) Buy information and take €50 regardless of its result.
E) Decline information and take €50.

:::

::: {#p01-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** A randomized label study detects a change in reported enjoyment but no reliable performance difference. Participants later say the label helped concentration; concentration was not independently measured. Which claim best fits?

A) The label had no effect on any unmeasured experience.
B) The label changed performance despite the reported comparison.
C) The label changed concentration, which mediated the rating effect.
D) The retrospective account identifies the participants' original causal process.
E) The label changed reported enjoyment; the concentration mechanism remains untested.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-p01)

::: {#answers-p01 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: E.**

- **A. Valuation, prediction, implementation (Incorrect)** The first is omission of an option; the third is weighting a consequence.
- **B. Implementation, learning, prediction (Incorrect)** The problems arise before implementation or outcome feedback.
- **C. Learning, option construction, valuation (Incorrect)** The first problem is not learning from an outcome.
- **D. Prediction, valuation, option construction (Incorrect)** This shifts each problem to the wrong stage.
- **E. Option construction, prediction, valuation (Correct)** The problems concern alternatives, consequences, and their importance respectively.

Review: [Chapter 1](../chapters/01-understanding-decision-making.qmd) · [Chapter 2](../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p01-01).

**Question 2: D.**

- **A. An inherited tradition determines the ethically best meal for everyone. (Incorrect)** Origins do not establish universal moral worth.
- **B. A meal has value only through its market price. (Incorrect)** Valuation also reflects identity, relationships, and experience.
- **C. A culturally learned value cannot influence a real preference. (Incorrect)** Learned meanings can shape subjective value.
- **D. The tradition helps explain the value; it does not settle what everyone ought to choose. (Correct)** Socially acquired meaning explains preferences without supplying a universal prescription.
- **E. A utility representation must ignore the meal's social meaning. (Incorrect)** Preference ordering can reflect consequences with social meaning.

Review: [Chapter 1](../chapters/01-understanding-decision-making.qmd) · [Chapter 6](../chapters/06-valuation.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p01-02).

**Question 3: D.**

- **A. Explain the selected job only after the contract is signed. (Incorrect)** Later justification does not repair the original comparison.
- **B. Ask applicants to ignore their personal travel preferences. (Incorrect)** Preferences over commuting remain relevant.
- **C. Increase the prominence of the highest salary further. (Incorrect)** This intensifies the original attentional imbalance.
- **D. Show salary and commuting time together on clearly labeled scales. (Correct)** Making both consequences interpretable helps them enter valuation.
- **E. Remove salary so that commuting becomes the only visible attribute. (Incorrect)** That replaces one incomplete comparison with another.

Review: [Chapter 3](../chapters/03-limited-attention.qmd) · [Chapter 6](../chapters/06-valuation.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p01-03).

**Question 4: C.**

- **A. Treat the central estimate as certain because it fits the current model. (Incorrect)** A plausible model prediction still carries uncertainty.
- **B. Refine an unrelated estimate that leaves the recommendation unchanged. (Incorrect)** Precision in an inconsequential input has less decision value.
- **C. Improve the consequential failure-rate estimate and compare outcomes across its plausible range. (Correct)** The consequential sensitivity and inexpensive informative check make this uncertainty worth investigating.
- **D. Average the suppliers' names to remove personal preference. (Incorrect)** The issue is uncertainty about consequences, not naming.
- **E. Stop analysis because a numerical recommendation already exists. (Incorrect)** A fragile consequential recommendation warrants a proportionate check.

Review: [Chapter 2](../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.qmd) · [Chapter 4](../chapters/04-predictive-mind.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p01-04).

**Question 5: A.**

- **A. The prediction may have altered the athlete's learning environment. (Correct)** Treatment induced by a forecast can help cause the outcome.
- **B. The prediction must have been consciously insincere. (Incorrect)** The coach can sincerely believe the forecast.
- **C. A correct forecast rules out effects of the coach's actions. (Incorrect)** Predictive success and causal influence can coexist.
- **D. Practice cannot be measured as part of a causal pathway. (Incorrect)** Practice is precisely a potentially measurable mediator.
- **E. The outcome supplies a direct measure of innate ability alone. (Incorrect)** Changed opportunities prevent that simple interpretation.

Review: [Chapter 4](../chapters/04-predictive-mind.qmd) · [Chapter 5](../chapters/05-expectations.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p01-05).

**Question 6: C.**

- **A. Compare premium beans with cheaper beans at their usual prices. (Incorrect)** Physical quality and price then vary together.
- **B. Replace tasting ratings with the retailer's preferred price. (Incorrect)** A preferred price does not measure the experience under study.
- **C. Randomly assign price labels to tasters served the same coffee. (Correct)** Identical coffee and random labels isolate the label manipulation.
- **D. Change both the price and serving temperature. (Incorrect)** Temperature becomes an additional explanation.
- **E. Ask only participants who already prefer expensive coffee. (Incorrect)** Selection limits the comparison and does not isolate the manipulation.

Review: [Chapter 4](../chapters/04-predictive-mind.qmd) · [Chapter 6](../chapters/06-valuation.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p01-06).

**Question 7: B.**

- **A. An action, an outcome, then a controlled experiment (Incorrect)** No controlled manipulation is described.
- **B. Perceptual inference, consequence forecast, then retrospective explanation (Correct)** The stages answer what is present, what will happen, and why a prior judgment was made.
- **C. A consequence forecast followed by two perceptual inferences (Incorrect)** Recognition comes first, and the final account concerns a prior judgment.
- **D. Three direct recordings of external reality (Incorrect)** Inference, forecasting, and explanation all involve interpretation.
- **E. Three judgments of the invitation's monetary value (Incorrect)** None is necessarily a valuation in money.

Review: [Chapter 4](../chapters/04-predictive-mind.qmd) · [Chapter 7](../chapters/07-rationalization.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p01-07).

**Question 8: D.**

- **A. Choose the higher salary because only money is comparable. (Incorrect)** Nonmonetary consequences can be valued and compared.
- **B. Assume flexibility has the same value for every applicant. (Incorrect)** The chapter emphasizes differences in subjective value.
- **C. Infer that the employer's first offer was irrational. (Incorrect)** Negotiability does not establish irrationality.
- **D. Evaluate the newly feasible salary–hours package against alternatives. (Correct)** Option construction and valuation should incorporate the negotiable trade-off.
- **E. Treat the original salary as a cost already paid. (Incorrect)** An offer is not an incurred sunk cost.

Review: [Chapter 2](../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.qmd) · [Chapter 6](../chapters/06-valuation.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p01-08).

**Question 9: A.**

- **A. Buy information; launch only on success, otherwise take €50. (Correct)** Perfect information yields 0.4×120 + 0.6×50 − 15 = €63, above €50.
- **B. Decline information and launch the product. (Incorrect)** Its expected profit is €48, below the certain €50.
- **C. Buy information and launch regardless of its result. (Incorrect)** This earns €48 − €15 = €33 in expectation.
- **D. Buy information and take €50 regardless of its result. (Incorrect)** This earns €35 and wastes the information.
- **E. Decline information and take €50. (Incorrect)** This misses the available €63 expected net payoff.

Review: [Chapter 2](../chapters/02-structuring-a-decision.qmd) · [Appendix A: decision analysis](../appendices/appendix-a-rational-choice-and-decision-analysis.qmd#rational-choice-and-decision-analysis). [Back to question 9](#p01-09).

**Question 10: E.**

- **A. The label had no effect on any unmeasured experience. (Incorrect)** Lack of measurement cannot establish no effect.
- **B. The label changed performance despite the reported comparison. (Incorrect)** The study did not reliably detect that difference.
- **C. The label changed concentration, which mediated the rating effect. (Incorrect)** The proposed mediator was neither independently measured nor manipulated.
- **D. The retrospective account identifies the participants' original causal process. (Incorrect)** A sincere account can be a post hoc explanation.
- **E. The label changed reported enjoyment; the concentration mechanism remains untested. (Correct)** The outcome comparison supports the rating effect, not the retrospective causal account.

Review: [Chapter 3](../chapters/03-limited-attention.qmd) · [Chapter 5](../chapters/05-expectations.qmd) · [Chapter 7](../chapters/07-rationalization.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p01-10).

:::
